claims.text: A conventional W–Cu composite can be produced by powder metallurgy with tungsten and copper phases forming a mechanically bonded microstructure.
Tungsten particles should be coated with a 50–100 nm nickel interlayer before composite consolidation.
The proposed effect should operate under high-temperature and irradiation conditions typical of fusion-reactor joints.
A nickel coating on tungsten particles reduces wettability problems between tungsten and copper.
A nickel coating enhances interfacial bonding between tungsten and copper.
A nickel coating eliminates interfacial voids in W–Cu composites.
Improved W–Cu interfacial bonding creates a more continuous electron-conduction pathway across the phases.
The nickel interlayer acts as a bridge that reduces thermal interface resistance between tungsten and copper.
Improved interfacial bonding minimizes phonon and electron scattering at the W–Cu interface.
Reduced interfacial scattering and thermal resistance increase the effective thermal conductivity of the composite.
The nickel interlayer maintains the structural integrity of the tungsten phase.
The nickel interlayer maintains the tungsten phase's resistance to irradiation-induced damage.
Nickel-coated tungsten particles may produce a greater than 10% increase in effective thermal conductivity relative to an otherwise comparable unmodified W–Cu composite.
The mechanical strength of the nickel-modified composite will remain comparable to that of the unmodified composite.
The irradiation resistance of the nickel-modified composite will remain comparable to that of the unmodified composite.
Bare tungsten particles in a copper matrix typically have imperfect interfacial bonding.
Imperfect W–Cu interfacial bonding produces higher thermal resistance.
The proposed effect requires the nickel coating to remain uniform and stable during sintering.
The nickel coating must be sufficiently thin to avoid forming a continuous secondary phase.
Processing must prevent excessive interdiffusion during high-temperature exposure for the proposed benefit to persist.

contradictions.description: The predicted improvement is described only as moderate and 'potentially >10%', but the falsification rule treats failure to exceed 10% as falsifying the hypothesis. An improvement of 10% or less could therefore be consistent with the stated prediction yet counted as falsification.
